751.event_title: Jacques Coeur, a furrier's son, is ennobled by Charles VII
751.event: Jacques Coeur, born around 1395 in Bourges as the son of a furrier, built a great trading business that dealt in salt, silks and many other goods. He became argentier (steward of royal expenditure) to King Charles VII, sat on the king's council, was put in charge of tax collection, and was ennobled in 1441. His fortune helped fund the king's reconquest of Normandy in 1450.
751.explanation: A merchant's son with no rank of his own was raised by his wealth into the king's council and the nobility of France.
751.tie_back: The kural says nothing but wealth turns those who count for nothing into people who count, and Coeur's fortune carried him from a furrier's household to the king's side.
751._accuracy_note: A clear case of wealth conferring standing, though Coeur's own ability, not just money, also earned him royal trust.

752.event_title: Twelve-year-old Charles Dickens works in a blacking factory while his father is in debtors' prison
752.event: In February 1824 John Dickens was imprisoned for debt in the Marshalsea prison in Southwark, and most of his family joined him there. His twelve-year-old son Charles was sent to work at Warren's Blacking warehouse near Hungerford Stairs, pasting labels on pots of boot blacking. The family was released some months later after an inheritance allowed the debt to be paid, and Dickens later drew on the debtors' prison in novels such as Little Dorrit.
752.explanation: The episode shows how quickly debt stripped a respectable family of its standing in Victorian society, and Dickens spent much of his writing life exposing how the poor were treated.
752.tie_back: The kural observes that everyone looks down on those who have nothing, and the Dickens family's fall into the Marshalsea and a child's labour in a rat-infested warehouse show that contempt in action.
752._accuracy_note: Illustrates the humiliation of poverty well, but the sources describe hardship rather than documenting specific acts of public scorn.

753.event_title: President Truman signs the Marshall Plan into law
753.place: Washington, D.C., United States, and Western Europe
753.event: President Harry Truman signed the Economic Cooperation Act, which created the European Recovery Program known as the Marshall Plan. Over about four years the United States transferred some 13 billion dollars in aid to sixteen Western European countries, including former wartime enemies, to rebuild their economies. Aid was also offered to the Soviet Union and the countries of eastern Europe, which declined to take part.
753.explanation: American wealth, sent abroad, helped rebuild war-shattered economies and turned recent battlefield enemies into partners.
753.tie_back: The kural calls wealth an unfailing lamp that dispels the darkness of hostility in any land its owner chooses, and Marshall aid carried that light into a Europe darkened by war.
753._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of wealth sent into foreign lands easing enmity, though the plan also had Cold War motives the kural does not address.

754.event_title: Shibusawa Eiichi publishes his book on ethics and business
754.event: Shibusawa Eiichi, who helped found Japan's First National Bank in 1873 and went on to help establish hundreds of companies, set out his business philosophy in the book Rongo to Soroban in 1916. Drawing on classical Chinese moral teaching, he argued that morality and economic activity are inseparable. He held that business should make profit by honest means and that its profits should serve the public good.
754.explanation: Shibusawa, often called the father of Japanese capitalism, insisted that wealth earned without ethics was no true success.
754.tie_back: The kural says wealth gained by knowing the right ways and without doing wrong gives birth to both virtue and happiness, which is almost exactly the union of moral teaching and the abacus (soroban) that Shibusawa taught.
754._accuracy_note: A close match: a builder of great wealth arguing publicly that wealth must be won by right means to be worth anything. Source swapped Oct 2026 (catalogue record confirms the 1916 publication; the "classical Chinese moral teaching" wording is from the earlier source and was not re-read).

755.event_title: The Kangxi Emperor freezes China's tax quota permanently
755.event: In 1712 the Kangxi Emperor of the Qing dynasty decreed that the empire's direct tax quota, tied to the count of adult males liable to tax, would be fixed at its existing level and never increased, even as the population grew. The policy is summed up in the phrase yongbu jiafu, never to add taxes. Economic historians note that the cap was largely observed for more than a century, so the tax burden per person fell as China's population and farmland grew; some scholarly accounts date the measure to 1713.
755.explanation: The emperor gave up revenue he could have raised, choosing light taxation of a growing population over a fuller treasury.
755.tie_back: The kural tells rulers to let go of wealth that does not come with compassion for the people, and Kangxi's freeze declined the extra revenue that heavier taxing of his subjects would have brought.
755._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial fit, since the sources document the policy and its effects rather than the emperor's motive of compassion.

756.event_title: Denmark collects the Sound Dues at Elsinore
756.event: From 1429 to 1857 the Danish crown required ships passing through the Oresund, the narrow strait between Denmark and Sweden that leads into the Baltic, to stop and pay a toll at Elsinore. Eric of Pomerania built the first fortress there in the 1420s, and Frederik II began the Renaissance castle of Kronborg in 1574. Around 1.8 million passages were recorded, and the toll was both a major source of royal income and a political instrument for Denmark.
756.explanation: For more than four centuries a single customs toll at a narrow strait helped finance the Danish monarchy.
756.tie_back: The kural lists toll and customs revenue among the lawful wealth of a king, and the Sound Dues are one of history's longest-running examples of exactly that kind of royal income.
756._accuracy_note: Illustrates one of the kural's three revenue sources (customs) very well, but not ownerless property or tribute.

757.event_title: Zubaydah funds wells and rest stations on the pilgrim road to Mecca
757.place: Darb Zubaydah, from Kufa (Iraq) to Mecca (Saudi Arabia)
757.event: Zubaydah bint Jafar, wife of the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid, supported charitable works along the pilgrimage road linking Kufa and Baghdad with Mecca. As growing numbers of pilgrims strained the water and food of the Arabian desert, she personally paid for many new intermediate rest stops for pilgrims travelling on foot, along with wells and reservoirs. The road became known as the Darb Zubaydah, and its Iraqi and Saudi sections are on UNESCO's World Heritage tentative list.
757.explanation: A royal fortune was turned into water and shelter for ordinary travellers, and the whole route came to bear her name.
757.tie_back: The kural calls compassion the child of love, raised by the wealthy foster-mother called wealth, and Zubaydah's riches gave her care for pilgrims the means to save lives across the desert.
757._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of wealth enabling compassion on a large scale, though her inner motives are not documented.

758.event_title: Heinrich Schliemann uses his merchant fortune to excavate Hisarlik
758.event: Heinrich Schliemann made a large fortune in trade, much of it as a military contractor during the Crimean War, and retired from business in his thirties to devote his money to archaeology. Frank Calvert, who owned part of the mound at Hisarlik and believed it was Troy, lacked the funds for further digging. Beginning in 1870, Schliemann paid for large excavations there himself, employing many workers, and he went on to uncover the remains of the ancient city.
758.explanation: Because he paid his own way, Schliemann could pursue an expensive, uncertain search that others could not afford to attempt.
758.tie_back: The kural says that one who starts a venture with money already in hand is like a person watching an elephant fight from a hilltop, and Schliemann's private fortune let him undertake the dig without depending on anyone.
758._accuracy_note: Fits the idea of a self-funded venture well, though Schliemann's crude methods and the origins of his wealth complicate him as a model.

759.event_title: Jakob Fugger finances the election of Charles V as Holy Roman Emperor
759.event: After Emperor Maximilian I died in 1519, his grandson Charles of Spain and King Francis I of France competed to be elected Holy Roman Emperor, and the electors sought payments from both. Of election expenses of about 852,000 guilders spent on Charles's behalf, the Augsburg banker Jakob Fugger raised almost 544,000. Charles was elected, and Francis I's bid failed.
759.explanation: A banker's money, not an army, decided which of Europe's two most powerful kings would wear the imperial crown.
759.tie_back: The kural says no steel is sharper than wealth for cutting down an enemy's pride, and Fugger's loans defeated the ambitions of the king of France without a blow being struck.
759._accuracy_note: A vivid demonstration of wealth defeating a proud rival, though it worked through the purchase of votes rather than honest means.

760.event_title: Banker Annamalai Chettiar founds Annamalai University
760.event: Annamalai Chettiar, from a Nattukottai Chettiar banking family whose business he expanded into South-East Asia, founded Sri Minakshi College and Tamil and Sanskrit colleges at Chidambaram in the early 1920s. In 1928 he agreed with the Madras government to hand these institutions over to form a university, and Annamalai University came into being on 1 January 1929, founded by a private philanthropist. He was knighted in 1923 and later received the hereditary title of Raja of Chettinad.
760.explanation: A fortune made in banking was turned into a university that promoted Tamil learning and served students across the region.
760.tie_back: The kural says that for those who have built up abundant, honestly earned wealth, virtue and happiness come easily, and Annamalai Chettiar's banking wealth made a lasting good work almost a matter of course.
760._accuracy_note: A good illustration of wealth flowing into virtue, with a Tamil connection; the sources describe the gift rather than the honesty of each earning.
